raw_text:
### Introduction and Epidemiology

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a life-threatening form of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) presenting during late pregnancy or the early postpartum months in women with no pre-existing heart disease [1,2]. The globally accepted diagnostic hallmark is a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) below 45% [1,2]. Although once considered an enigmatic pathology [5], research has significantly advanced our understanding of its etiology and clinical course [3]. PPCM shows notable geographical and racial variations; Black women in the United States and sub-Saharan Africa suffer from a higher incidence, more severe presentations, and lower recovery rates [4,12]. Global registry data indicate that socio-economic status also plays a significant role in determining maternal and neonatal prognosis [22,29].

### Pathophysiology: The Hormonal-Vascular-Genetic Interplay

The pathogenesis of PPCM is characterized by a "two-hit" interplay of vascular and hormonal insults on a genetically predisposed background [3,4]. A key pathway involves oxidative stress-mediated cleavage of the pituitary hormone prolactin (23 kDa) by cathepsin D into a toxic 16 kDa fragment [6]. This 16 kDa prolactin derivative promotes endothelial apoptosis, capillary rarefaction, and myocardial dysfunction, partly by upregulating microRNA-146a [6,14]. A key clinical risk factor is preeclampsia, which shares a pathogenetic link of angiogenic imbalance [11]; placental secretion of soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1) induces widespread endothelial damage by neutralizing vascular endothelial growth factor (VEF) [10,13]. Genetic susceptibility represents the other major driver; approximately 10% to 15% of patients carry truncating variants in the titin gene (*TTNtv*), which overlaps genetically with familial dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) [7,19]. Autoantibodies directed against cardiac sarcomeric proteins further highlight an autoimmune facet in some patients [15].

### Clinical Presentation and Diagnosis

PPCM symptoms (dyspnea, orthopnea, fatigue, and edema) frequently mimic normal physiological changes of late pregnancy, causing diagnostic delays that impair myocardial recovery [12,18]. Serial biomarker testing (e.g., NT-proBNP) is valuable for screening [3]. Echocardiography remains the gold standard for diagnosing left ventricular dysfunction [1,2]. Data from the EURObservational Research Programme (EORP) PPCM registry demonstrate that baseline right ventricular involvement and severe left ventricular remodeling predict poor clinical outcomes and lower recovery rates at six months, as assessed by contemporary prognostic scores [16,21,30].

### Therapeutic Management and Evolving Strategies

Therapeutic management is highly dependent on pregnancy status [18]. During gestation, guideline-directed medical therapies (GDMT) such as ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors (ARNIs), mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs), and SGLT2 inhibitors are strictly contraindicated due to fetal toxicity [3,18]. Antepartum HFrEF therapy is restricted to metoprolol succinate, hydralazine, nitrates, and loop diuretics [1,18]. Postpartum, GDMT should be rapidly optimized [3]. While ARNIs were traditionally avoided during lactation, recent evidence suggests that the transfer of sacubitril/valsartan into breast milk is negligible, which may expand therapeutic options [25]. Levosimendan offers safe inotropic support in acute decompensation [27]. In patients with severe dysfunction (LVEF < 35%), a wearable cardioverter-defibrillator (WCD) is recommended to protect against sudden cardiac death during the high-risk recovery phase [17,26]. Refractory cases may require mechanical circulatory support or heart transplantation [17,28].

Pathogenesis-targeted therapy with bromocriptine, a dopamine D2 receptor agonist that inhibits prolactin secretion, has shown considerable success [6,8]. A multicenter randomized trial demonstrated high rates of LVEF recovery and excellent survival with bromocriptine [9]. These findings were corroborated by a large-scale analysis of the EORP PPCM registry, which associated bromocriptine use with improved maternal recovery and clinical outcomes [23]. Because bromocriptine raises thromboembolic risks, concurrent anticoagulation is mandatory [9,17].

### Prognosis and Subsequent Pregnancies

Although up to 70% of women achieve myocardial recovery within six months [10,21], those with persistent dysfunction face chronic heart failure risks [3,30]. Pre-conception counseling is vital for subsequent pregnancies, which carry a high risk of relapse, particularly in women who fail to fully recover their LVEF (≥ 50%) beforehand [20,24]. Managed care by a multidisciplinary cardio-obstetric team is crucial to optimize long-term maternal survival [5,24].
